title: ～わけにはいかない — “can’t (afford to) ～”
summary: Says you cannot do something because of social duty, common sense or circumstances, even if you might want to. It attaches to the dictionary form of a verb (or ない-form for the opposite: ないわけにはいかない). Not about physical ability.

patterns.form: 動詞辞書形＋わけにはいかない
patterns.gloss: can’t do ～ (because of circumstances or duty)

patterns.form: 動詞ない形＋ないわけにはいかない

body.p: The speaker has a reason, such as an exam tomorrow or an important promise, that makes the action unacceptable. 休むわけにはいかない: I may want to rest, but I can’t.
～ないわけにはいかない reverses it: 行かないわけにはいかない means “I can’t not go”, i.e. “I have to go.” This is a common way to say obligation politely.
できない states ability or possibility. ～わけにはいかない says that the situation or social rule does not allow it, even if you are physically able. The reason is usually stated just before.

examples.ja: 明日（あした）は試験（しけん）だから、休（やす）むわけにはいかない。
examples.romaji: Ashita wa shiken da kara, yasumu wake niwa ikanai.
examples.tr: Tomorrow is the exam, so I can’t afford to take a day off.

examples.ja: 大事（だいじ）な約束（やくそく）だから、遅（おく）れるわけにはいかない。
examples.romaji: Daiji na yakusoku da kara, okureru wake niwa ikanai.
examples.tr: It’s an important appointment, so I can’t afford to be late.

examples.ja: みんなが待（ま）っているので、ここで諦（あきら）めるわけにはいかない。
examples.romaji: Minna ga matte iru node, koko de akirameru wake niwa ikanai.
examples.tr: Everyone is waiting, so I can’t just give up here.

pitfalls: Use the dictionary form before わけ (休むわけにはいかない). Do not use it for plain inability (e.g. “can’t swim”): use できない.
ないわけにはいかない means “must”, not “must not”. Watch the double negative.
